title: Hunter API: Endpoints, Credit Costs and Pricing (2026)
summary: Hunter API pricing plans scale based on email lookups, domain searches, and verification requests. Identify your usage tier to determine monthly costs.
body_markdown:
## Running Hunter lookups in Activepieces workflows


When the work starts from a form submission or a CRM record rather than from a user action in your product, a workflow tool is the right home for Hunter lookups.


The person paged when it fails is then an operations owner, not your application's on-call engineer.


### When a workflow beats custom code


[Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com/blog/is-activepieces-free-automation-plans-and-limits) is an MIT-licensed core with 746 integrations, and a run is 1 credit however many steps the flow has, so a Hunter flow that finds, verifies and writes back costs the same as one that only finds.


Unlimited flows on every plan, including free, means splitting the work into small steps never changes the bill.


When a verification call fails or comes back unusable, you open the run and see the exact input and output of each step, instead of grepping application logs for a request you never tagged.


Your Hunter key is the credential this article keeps asking someone to own, and Activepieces lets you keep it out of its database entirely: on the self-hosted edition and the enterprise cloud tier, connection secrets can be routed to your own secret manager.


Point a self-hosted instance at one and the key won't appear in the Activepieces database, which you can inspect yourself; Zapier and Make keep connection credentials in their own cloud. MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run Activepieces in production.


Keep direct code for anything a customer touches inside your product. A signup form that must reject a bad address in the moment belongs behind your server route, with your own limits and error handling.


A workflow suits the back-office cases: leads arriving from a form, records created in a CRM, a nightly sweep of unverified contacts. Those tolerate a delay, and the people who own them aren't engineers.


### Verify-on-arrival pattern with the key stored as a connection


The pattern has four steps:


1. A trigger fires when a form entry or CRM record arrives.
2. A step sends the email address to Hunter's verification endpoint.
3. A branch reads the returned status and decides what the record is.
4. A final step writes that status back onto the record.


Store the Hunter key as a connection, not pasted into a step, so it lives in one place and a departing contractor's flow doesn't carry a copy of it. Name an owner for that connection when you create it.


In the screenshot below, a completed run in Activepieces shows the trigger and its single HTTP step both carrying green checkmarks. The step's panel lists its duration, the JSON request sent with its Authorization header, and the response with a 200 status.


That's the evidence you want per call, since it lets you tell a Hunter failure from a mapping error without guessing.


Next, add the retry and failure handling deliberately: a retried step spends credits again, so decide how many attempts a record gets before the flow stops and flags it.
